_link.title: I can describe how the rate of a reaction can be monitored by measuring changes in concentration over time

toLevel2.stem: What happens to the concentration of a reactant as a reaction proceeds?
What happens to the concentration of a product as a reaction proceeds?
How can the rate of a chemical reaction be monitored?
toLevel2.answer: By measuring concentration changes over time
distractors: By measuring the colour of the container
By counting the number of atoms present
By measuring the mass of the container

toLevel2.stem: On a concentration-time graph, a steeper curve indicates:
The unit commonly used for concentration when measuring reaction rate is:
Reaction rate can be determined by measuring the decrease in concentration of a reactant over time.
The concentration of a product decreases as a reaction progresses.
Reaction rate can be measured by tracking how the concentration of a {{blank:1}} decreases or the concentration of a {{blank:2}} increases over time.
A concentration-time graph for a reactant shows a {{blank:1}} in concentration, while a graph for a product shows an {{blank:2}}.
To monitor reaction rate, concentration is measured at regular {{blank:1}} intervals and recorded in units of {{blank:2}}.

toLevel3.stem: Why does the concentration of a reactant decrease over time during a reaction?
toLevel3.answer: Reactant particles are consumed as they form products
distractors: Reactant particles evaporate from the solution
The volume of the solution increases over time
Reactant particles gain mass during the reaction

toLevel3.stem: On a concentration-time graph for a reactant, what does a curve that levels off indicate?
toLevel3.answer: The reaction is slowing down and approaching completion
distractors: The reaction is speeding up over time
The concentration of products has stopped increasing

toLevel3.stem: Why is measuring the change in concentration over time a useful method for determining reaction rate?
toLevel3.answer: It directly shows how fast reactants are consumed or products are formed
distractors: It measures the temperature change of the system accurately
It determines the activation energy of the reaction precisely
It indicates whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic

toLevel3.stem: What does the gradient of a concentration-time graph represent?
toLevel3.answer: The rate of reaction at that point
distractors: The activation energy of the reaction
The total amount of product formed
The enthalpy change of the reaction

toLevel3.stem: A fast reaction and a slow reaction both start with the same initial concentration of reactant. How would their concentration-time graphs compare?
toLevel3.answer: The fast reaction shows a steeper initial decline
distractors: The slow reaction shows a steeper initial decline
Both graphs would look identical in shape
The fast reaction starts at a lower concentration

toLevel3.stem: Why does the rate of reaction typically slow down as the reaction proceeds?
toLevel3.answer: The concentration of reactants decreases, reducing collision frequency
distractors: The activation energy increases as the reaction continues
The products inhibit further collisions between reactants
The temperature of the system drops as energy is consumed

toLevel3.stem: A steeper gradient on a reactant concentration-time graph indicates a faster rate of reaction.
As a reaction progresses, the rate typically {{blank:1}} because the concentration of {{blank:2}} decreases.
The gradient of a concentration-time graph at any point gives the {{blank:1}} rate of the reaction at that {{blank:2}}.
A fast reaction has a {{blank:1}} gradient on a concentration-time graph compared to a {{blank:2}} reaction.

toLevel4.stem: A student measures the concentration of a reactant at 0 s (0.50 M) and at 20 s (0.30 M). What is the average rate of reaction over this interval?
In an experiment, a student plots the concentration of a product over time and obtains a curve that rises steeply then levels off. What does the levelling off indicate?
toLevel4.answer: The reactants are nearly used up and the reaction is approaching completion
distractors: The reaction has reversed and products are converting back to reactants
The temperature of the reaction mixture has dropped below the threshold
The catalyst has been consumed and can no longer assist the reaction

toLevel4.stem: A student wants to compare the rates of two reactions. They measure the concentration of a reactant every 10 seconds for both. Which feature of the resulting graphs should they compare?
toLevel4.answer: The steepness of the curves at corresponding time intervals
distractors: The colour of the solutions at the start of the reaction
The final temperature reached by each reaction mixture
The total number of data points collected for each reaction

toLevel4.stem: A reaction produces aqueous iodine, which turns a starch indicator blue-black. A student measures the time taken for the colour change to appear. What concentration change are they indirectly monitoring?
toLevel4.answer: The increase in iodine concentration until it reaches a detectable level
distractors: The decrease in starch concentration as it is consumed by iodine
The increase in reactant concentration as the solution is heated
The decrease in water concentration as the reaction proceeds

toLevel4.stem: A student records: [Reactant] = 0.80 M at t = 0 s and [Reactant] = 0.40 M at t = 40 s. What is the average reaction rate?

Two experiments use the same reaction but different starting concentrations. Experiment A starts at 1.0 M and Experiment B at 0.5 M. Both are measured over 60 s. How would you expect their concentration-time graphs to differ?
toLevel4.answer: Experiment A starts higher and initially declines more steeply
distractors: Experiment B starts higher and declines more steeply
Both graphs will be identical in shape and position
Experiment A will show an increasing concentration curve

toLevel4.stem: A student draws a tangent to the concentration-time curve at t = 10 s and calculates its gradient. What does this value represent?
toLevel4.answer: The instantaneous rate of reaction at t = 10 s
distractors: The average rate over the first 10 seconds
The activation energy of the reaction at t = 10 s
The total concentration change from 0 to 10 seconds

toLevel4.stem: A reactant concentration drops from 0.60 M to 0.20 M in 20 seconds. The average rate is {{blank:1}} mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹, calculated using the formula rate = {{blank:2}}.
To find the instantaneous rate at a specific time, a student draws a {{blank:1}} to the curve and calculates its {{blank:2}}.
When comparing two reactions, the one with the {{blank:1}} initial gradient on a concentration-time graph has the {{blank:2}} initial rate.

toLevel5.stem: A concentration-time graph for a reactant shows a curve that decreases rapidly at first, then gradually levels off. What can be inferred about the rate of reaction over time?
toLevel5.answer: The rate is highest at the start and decreases as reactants are consumed
distractors: The rate is constant throughout the entire reaction period
The rate increases as the reaction approaches completion
The rate is zero at the start and increases over time

toLevel5.stem: A student measures the concentration of a product every 5 seconds and plots the results. The curve rises steeply for the first 15 seconds, then becomes almost flat. What does the flat section suggest about reactant concentration?
toLevel5.answer: Most of the reactant has been consumed so little further reaction occurs
distractors: The reactant concentration is increasing during the flat section
The reactant has started to form a precipitate and cannot be measured
The reaction has reversed and products are converting back to reactants

toLevel5.stem: Two students monitor the same reaction. Student A measures reactant concentration and Student B measures product concentration. Both plot their data on the same time axis. How do their graphs relate?
toLevel5.answer: They are mirror images — one decreases while the other increases
distractors: Both graphs show identical decreasing curves over time
Both graphs show identical increasing curves over time
The graphs have no relationship to each other at all

toLevel5.stem: A student claims that measuring concentration at only two time points is sufficient to fully describe the rate of a reaction. Evaluate this claim.
toLevel5.answer: It gives only the average rate and misses how the rate changes over time
distractors: It is fully sufficient because rate is constant throughout a reaction
It is sufficient because concentration changes linearly with time
It is insufficient only because the equipment is not precise enough

toLevel5.stem: A student argues that monitoring product concentration is always better than monitoring reactant concentration for determining rate. Is this valid?
toLevel5.answer: No — either can be used depending on which is easier to measure accurately
distractors: Yes — product concentration always gives more accurate rate values
Yes — reactant concentration cannot be measured during a reaction
No — only reactant concentration can be used for rate calculations

toLevel5.stem: A student calculates the average rate over 60 seconds and finds it is 0.015 mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹. The instantaneous rate at t = 5 s is 0.040 mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹. What explains this difference?
toLevel5.answer: The rate decreases over time, so the early rate is higher than the average
distractors: The student made an error in calculating the instantaneous rate
Average rate is always higher than instantaneous rate at any point
The reaction sped up after 5 seconds causing the average to decrease

toLevel5.stem: A student suggests that taking more frequent concentration measurements will improve the accuracy of rate calculations. Under what condition is this most true?
toLevel5.answer: When the rate changes rapidly and few data points could miss the variation
distractors: When the reaction is very slow and the rate is effectively constant
When the reaction occurs in a closed system with no gas production
When the concentration of the catalyst changes during the reaction

toLevel5.stem: In a reaction, the reactant concentration drops from 1.0 M to 0.1 M. A student notes that most of the decrease occurs in the first 20% of the total reaction time. What does this suggest?
toLevel5.answer: The reaction rate is much faster at higher reactant concentrations
distractors: The reaction has a very low activation energy at the start only
A catalyst was present only during the first 20% of the reaction
The temperature was higher at the start and decreased over time

toLevel5.stem: The average rate over an interval can differ from the {{blank:1}} rate at a specific time because the rate {{blank:2}} as reactants are consumed.
Monitoring {{blank:1}} concentration or {{blank:2}} concentration can both be used to determine reaction rate, depending on which is easier to measure.
